'''''Malva pusilla''''', also known as '''''Malva rotundifolia''''' (the latter of which is now officially rejected by botanists){{Citation needed|reason=Weasel words|date=January 2022}}, the '''low mallow''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=MAPU5|taxon=Malva pusilla|accessdate=27 January 2016}}</ref> '''small mallow''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007|accessdate=2014-10-17}}</ref> or the '''round-leaved mallow''', is an annual and biennial herb species of the Mallow [[genus]] ''[[Malva]]'' in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] of [[Malvaceae]]. Malva is a genus that consists of about 30 species of plants. This genus consists of plants named mallows. Mallows grow in many regions, including temperate, subtropical, and tropical areas.<ref name=luontoportti>{{cite web|title=Dwarf Mallow|url=http://www.luontoportti.com/suomi/en/kukkakasvit/dwarf-mallow|work=NatureGate|accessdate=19 October 2013}}</ref>

==Distribution==
''Malva pusilla'' is native to temperate and Mediterranean Europe, Turkey, Caucasia, and northwest Iran.<ref name=malva>{{cite web|last=Hinsley|first=Stewart R.|title=Malvaceae Info|url=http://www.malvaceae.info/|accessdate=19 October 2013}}</ref> It is invasive to North America, Europe, and Korea.<ref name=CABI>{{cite web|title=Malva pusilla|url=http://www.cabi.org/isc/?compid=5&dsid=115483&loadmodule=datasheet&page=481&site=144|work=Invasive Species Compendium|publisher=CABI|accessdate=19 October 2013|date=30 August 2013}}</ref> In the United States, in can specifically be found in the states of California, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Massachusetts, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, North Dakota, Nebraska, New Mexico, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia, Wisconsin and Wyoming.<ref name=sagebud>{{cite web|title=Low Mallow (Malva Pusilla)|url=http://sagebud.com/low-mallow-malva-pusilla/|work=Sagebud|accessdate=19 October 2013}}</ref> 
[[File:Malva pusilla distribution.png|right|thumb|"Invasive distribution of Malva pusilla in North America"]]

==Habitat and ecology==
''Malva pusilla'' can be found widely in wastelands, grasslands, pastures, and by roadsides.<ref name="Garms, Harry 1967">{{cite book|last=Garms|first=Harry|title=The Natural History of Europe All in Color|year=1967|publisher=Paul Hamlyn|author2=Wilhelm Eigener |author3=A. Melderis |author4=Joyce Pope }}</ref> It is easy to grow in ordinary garden conditions in moist, fertile soil and a sunny setting. It is prone to predation by rabbits and infestation by rust fungus.<ref name="pfaf">{{cite web | url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Malva+pusilla | title=Malva pusilla – Sm. | work=Plants for a Future | accessdate=19 October 2013}}</ref>

==Invasiveness==
Mallows can be used as garden flowers. However, some species may be considered weeds, especially in areas where they are not native. ''Malva pusilla'' grows rapidly as a weed in gardens and farmlands. It is considered hard to get rid of because of its long and tough taproots. Among cultivated crops, it can be very competitive and it can spread very quickly. Herbicide control options of this mallow are limited and not highly effective.<ref name=mb>{{cite web|title=Round-leaved Mallow|url=https://www.gov.mb.ca/agriculture/crops/weeds/fab12s00.html|work=Manitoba Agriculture, Food and Rural Initiatives|publisher=Manitoba|accessdate=19 October 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131020133649/http://www.gov.mb.ca/agriculture/crops/weeds/fab12s00.html|archive-date=20 October 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Morphology==
''Malva pusilla'' stems can grow to a height of {{convert|4|-|20|in}}. ''Malva pusilla'' leaves are attached alternately to the stem. Leaves have orbicular shape (widely triangular) with palmate venation and serrate margins. In the past, mallows were often referred to as cheesepants because the carpel is shaped similarly to a triangular wedge of cheese.<ref name="luontoportti" />

==Flowers and seeds==
The ''Malva pusilla'' flower consists of five petals of white, sometimes pale pink, color with pink venation. Petals and calyx are about the same length.<ref name="Garms, Harry 1967"/> It has many stamens and the filaments are fused. Flowering begins in June and July and ends in September and October. Flowers bloom in groups of 2 to 5 at the base of the leaf stalks. The flower's nectar is located near the upper surface of the sepals. It is self-pollinating with the aid of insects.<ref name="luontoportti" /> The flowers are hermaphrodite, consisting of both female and male parts.<ref name="pfaf" /> There are usually 8 to 12 seeds per flower that are arranged in a ring. The tough seed coat enables it to remain dormant in the soil for up to 100 years. Seeds tend to germinate late in the springtime during temperatures of {{convert|15|-|20|C}}.<ref name=mb />

==Uses==
===Dyes===
Dyes can be obtained from the ''Malva pusilla'' plant and seed heads, such as cream, yellow, and green. The root can also be used as a toothbrush.<ref name="pfaf" />

===Food===
Some species of mallows are eaten as a leaf vegetable. The leaves and seeds of ''Malva pusilla'' are edible. They have a mild and pleasant flavor that can be used in salads.<ref name="pfaf" /> Known in Arabic as ''khobeza'' ({{langx|ar|خُبَيْزَة}} {{transliteration|ar|ALA|khubayzah}}, literally 'small bread'), it serves as [[famine food]]. In April 2024, the ''New York Times'' reported that Gazans under siege were eating it to stave off starvation. <ref>{{cite news |author1=Ben Hubbard |author2=Bilal Shbair |title=Gazans Are Turning to This Wild Plant for Survival |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/04/07/world/middleeast/gaza-hunger-food-khobeza.html |access-date=11 April 2024 |work=New York Times |date=April 7, 2024 |page=1}}</ref>

===Medicinal===
''Malva pusilla'' has medicinal uses. The leaves are [[demulcent]], which can be used as a soothing agent to relieve minor pain and membrane inflammation. They can be used to treat inflammation of the [[Digestive system|digestive]] and [[urinary system]]s. The seed of the ''Malva pusilla'' can be used in the treatment of coughs, [[bronchitis]], [[ulcer]]s, and [[hemorrhoid]]s. It can also be applied externally to treat diseases of the skin. Although there have been no indications of dangerous toxicity, the leaves of ''Malva pusilla'' can be highly concentrated in nitrates, which can be dangerous to animals.<ref name="pfaf" />

==Cross hybridization==
Extensive [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridization]] can be done within the Mallow [[genus]] ''[[Malva]]''. A cross between ''Malva pusilla'' and ''Malva neglecta'' is ''Malva ×henningii''. A cross between ''Malva pusilla'' and ''Malva sylvestris'' is ''Malva ×littoralis''.<ref name=malva />
